{"url": "https://export.arxiv.org/api/query?search_query=all%3Amapping+causal+state+reconstruction+error+to+information-theoretic+dissipation+bounds+under+coarse-grained+observation&max_results=4", "scope": "paper abstracts; preprints, peer-review status not verified", "excerpt": "title: Quantum Coarse-Graining: An Information-Theoretic Approach to Thermodynamics
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/1607.03104v1
published: 2016-07-11T16:00:51Z
summary: We investigate fundamental connections between thermodynamics and quantum information theory. First, we show that the operational framework of thermal operations is nonequivalent to the framework of Gibbs-preserving maps, and we comment on this gap. We then introduce a fully information-theoretic framework generalizing the above by making further abstraction of physical quantities such as energy. It is technically convenient to work with and reproduces known results for finite-size quantum thermodynamics. With our framework we may determine the minimal work cost of implementing any logical process. In the case of information processing on memory registers with a degenerate Hamiltonian, the answer is given by the max-entropy, a measure of information known from quantum information theory. In the general case, we obtain a new information measure, the "coherent relative entropy", which generalizes both the conditional entropy and the relative entropy. It satisfies a collection of properties which justifies its interpretation as an entropy measure and which connects it to known quantities. We then present how, from our framework, macroscopic thermodynamics emerges by typicality, after singling out an appropriate class of thermodynamic states possessing some suitable reversibility property. A natural thermodynamic potential emerges, dictating possible state transformations, and whose differential describes the physics of the system. The textbook thermodynamics of a gas is recovered as well as the form of the second law relating thermodynamic entropy and heat exchange. Finally, noting that quantum states are relative to the observer, we see that the procedure above gives rise to a natural form of coarse-graining in quantum mechanics: Each observer can consistently apply the formalism of quantum information according to their own fundamental unit of information.

title: Basic Types of Coarse-Graining
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0602024v2
published: 2006-02-01T15:18:12Z
summary: We consider two basic types of coarse-graining: the Ehrenfests' coarse-graining and its extension to a general principle of non-equilibrium thermodynamics, and the coarse-graining based on uncertainty of dynamical models and Epsilon-motions (orbits). Non-technical discussion of basic notions and main coarse-graining theorems are presented: the theorem about entropy overproduction for the Ehrenfests' coarse-graining and its generalizations, both for conservative and for dissipative systems, and the theorems about stable properties and the Smale order for Epsilon-motions of general dynamical systems including structurally unstable systems. Computational kinetic models of macroscopic dynamics are considered. We construct a theoretical basis for these kinetic models using generalizations of the Ehrenfests' coarse-graining. General theory of reversible regularization and filtering semigroups in kinetics is presented, both for linear and non-linear filters. We obtain explicit expressions and entropic stability conditions for filtered equations. A brief discussion of coarse-graining by rounding and by small noise is also presented.

title: Contextual Information Allocation in Shared-State Cognitive Models: An Information-Theoretic Bound
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2602.16716v4
published: 2026-02-03T19:20:10Z
summary: Context-sensitive behavior can be modeled by enriching an internal state, by allowing a response rule to access context directly, or by preserving a shared state while introducing an auxiliary criterion or control variable. This paper isolates an information-theoretic constraint on the third architecture. Let $C$ denote context, $S$ a candidate internal or latent state, $O$ an observable response, and $M$ an auxiliary variable such that $O\perp C\mid(S,M)$. Then \[ I(C;O\mid S)\le I(C;M\mid S)\le H(M\mid S). \] Once a shared state has been specified, residual context dependence in behavior therefore lower-bounds both the context information and the conditional entropy that an auxiliary context-mediating mechanism must carry. The bound is representation-relative rather than a measure of state-space size or a universal contextuality measure. A worked recognition-memory example shows how the quantity can be computed for payoff-induced criterion shifts and compared across alternative representational allocations. Ontological contextuality and quantum probability are treated as a separate specialization rather than as prerequisites for the cognitive interpretation. More broadly, the framework provides a basis for analyzing context-memory-control trade-offs in cognitive models and artificial agents that must maintain coherent behavior across changing contexts under bounded internal representations.

title: The classical limit of quantum mechanics through coarse-grained measurements
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2503.15642v2
published: 2025-03-19T18:59:58Z
summary: Understanding how classical physics emerges from quantum mechanics remains a central problem in the foundations of physics. Here we derive a classical limit from finite-resolution measurements, modeled by continuous coarse-grained POVMs. When the resolved phase-space area is large compared with Planck's constant, the accessible statistics of any quantum state admit an effective classical description: coarse-grained observables become approximately jointly measurable and the induced probability density is positive. We derive the exact evolution equation for this density and show that, in the strong coarse-graining regime, its non-Liouville corrections are suppressed up to an Ehrenfest time, resulting in classical Hamiltonian flow generated by a Hamiltonian smoothed over the measurement cell. When the Hamiltonian varies negligibly across such a cell, the smoothed Hamiltonian reduces to the classical Hamiltonian whose quantization produced the quantum dynamics, thereby closing the quantization--classical-limit loop. Repeated finite-resolution measurements then generate stochastic records confined, with high probability, to tubes around classical trajectories. Our results provide a unified operational framework for the quantum-to-classical transition in microscopic and macroscopic systems, and establish the consistency of the quantization--classical-limit cycle.", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "28b489891f3de30979ab671b4715233d5c1ce9b451ae62c95e3fcf225b8f9c36", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "causal_memory", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["arxiv:1607.03104v1", "arxiv:2602.16716v4", "arxiv:2503.15642v2"], "source_candidates": [], "source_candidate_identities": {}}

article.body:
Research teams have been mapping how physical systems hold traces of their history, specifically looking at causal memory. This means a system’s present state helps predict future outcomes. Researchers used coarse-graining, which is an analogy like looking at a pointillist painting from across the room where individual dots blur into a coherent shape, to simplify complex systems and study their memory. Recent readings suggest that this process of simplifying information fundamentally limits how accurately we can reconstruct a system's history. It turns out that maintaining reliable memory is not free; it requires specific energy inputs, and there is a direct trade-off between the precision of the record and the energy the system loses during the process. Some interpretations suggest this link is universal for physical systems, while others argue it depends heavily on how the system is driven by outside forces [1]. Our focus shifted to how these individual memories become public facts, or objective records. An objective record is one that many independent observers can agree upon, regardless of their own viewpoint. To understand this, imagine a news broadcast reaching thousands of listeners; the information is the same for everyone, regardless of where they are standing. Researchers found that this reliability comes from redundancy, where the environment copies a system's state into multiple, independent parts. This ensures the information is robust, meaning it does not vanish easily. We looked at how this happens even when quantum scrambling tries to hide or delocalize information across a system. The records persist because of specific patterns called spectrum broadcast structures, which effectively lock that information into the surrounding environment [2]. Finally, the group investigated whether chemistry itself acts as a memory device. They studied autocatalytic networks, which are chemical systems that sustain themselves. An analogy is a chain reaction where the products of a chemical step act as catalysts to speed up the creation of more of those same products, allowing the system to keep running. Researchers are using algebraic math to look at stoichiometric submatrices, essentially grids representing the proportions of ingredients, to see if these networks can hold stable, history-dependent states without modern DNA. The findings suggest that these systems might hit a threshold where simple chemical persistence turns into something resembling heredity, but this remains theoretical. The distinction between simple state-holding and true template-copying is still a major point of discussion within our group, as we struggle to verify if these theoretical patterns hold up in active flow-reactor experiments [3]. This leaves us with a persistent uncertainty: At what precise threshold does a system shift from merely holding a history to actively creating a lineage that can adapt?

Summary

Our group examined how physical systems keep records of the past. We found that simplifying a system to understand it usually costs energy and limits accuracy. We also studied how information spreads through an environment so that many people can see the same facts, even when the system is jumbled. Finally, we looked at chemical networks that act like a self-sustaining loop. While these systems can remember their own history, we still do not know exactly when they cross the line into becoming capable of evolving.
article.lede: Our latest research explores the physical limits of memory storage, how information becomes publicly accessible, and whether chemical networks can sustain historical records.
article.lens: This checkpoint synthesizes research on the energetic cost of memory, the emergence of objective facts via environmental redundancy, and the potential for autocatalytic chemical networks to function as primitive hereditary systems.
article.title: Progress in Mapping Physical, Objective, and Chemical Memory
